title: America's Most Haunted Highways
excerpt: As Halloween approaches, it’s the specters and ghouls haunting America’s highways that give us the chills.
content:
Stay up to speed with stories written by drivers, for drivers.

Get automotive news, DIY tips, market trends, in-depth car profiles, and more right in your email inbox.

America’s roads can be scary places at the best of times. We’ve got distracted drivers texting, while others simply let their cars drive themselves, relying on technology that’s constantly beta-testing. Then there are the robotaxis, with nobody behind the wheel at all.

However, at this time of year our thoughts turn to the supernatural. As Halloween approaches, it’s the specters and ghouls haunting America’s highways that send shivers down our spines.

Every state has its ghost stories—tales of treacherous curves, grisly murders, and evil spirits that terrorize the roads. Would you dare drive these haunted highways?

Highway 299, California

On Highway 299, there’s a literal ghost town. During the Gold Rush of the 1850s, Whiskeytown and “Old Shasta” both boomed, but the area was flooded in 1962, and Whiskeytown was lost beneath the waters. The ruins of Shasta’s blacksmith, bakery, and courthouse remain, and it’s here that the ghosts of hanged criminals are said to roam. At Whiskeytown Lake, the spirits of former residents haunt the area.

Riverdale Road, Colorado

On this meandering road just outside of Denver, drivers report sightings of the Lady in White. This ghostly hitchhiker wanders Riverdale Road dressed in a billowing white dress. Sometimes she disappears before getting a ride; on other occasions, she walks off into the woods. Locals believe that she may be the specter of a bride who died in a car accident, while others suggest that she was killed in the nearby David Wolpert House. Adding to the mysteries of this road are claims of a ghostly Camaro with only one headlight that challenges other drivers to race, and a ghoulish jogger who taps on the windows of passing cars.

Spooksville Triangle: Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma

At the triangle of roads around Interstate 44 at Joplin, Missouri; Columbus, Kansas; and Miami, Oklahoma, drivers report a myriad of mysterious goings-on. Most famous are the inexplicable bouncing red and yellow orbs of light, known as the Joplin or Tri-State Spook, that float in the sky. There are also claims of phantom cars that tailgate drivers and hitchhikers who disappear.

U.S. 31, Michigan

Petoskey, Michigan, is known for two legends. The first is Ernest Hemingway, who spent his youthful summers by the lake. The second is Luke the Spook. According to Native American lore, Luke is a shape-shifting Skinwalker, Wendigo, or Waheela, whose glowing eyes are often seen spying from the woods. Rumor has it that in the 1950s, a teen chased after Luke after frightening the young fellow’s girlfriend. Luke attacked the teen, felling him with a single blow from a clawed hand and leaving the teen scarred for life.

Kancamagus Highway, New Hampshire

The Kancamagus Highway is a crackingly curvaceous section of New Hampshire Route 112 that cuts through the White Mountain Forest. In the fall, there’s the added charm of watching the trees turn colors in a fashion even more dramatic than the bends of the road. However, there’s a darker side to the Kanc. Back in the fall of 1891, local resident Thomas Colbath, then 41 years old, left his farm one afternoon to do some chores. He did not return. His wife, Ruth, lit a lamp in the window of their home every day for the next 39 years until she died. Three years later, Thomas finally came home with no explanation for his disappearance, only to find his house sold. Once again, he disappeared and was never seen again.

Kelly Road, Pennsylvania

Kelly Road’s Mystery Mile in Pennsylvania between Industry and Ohioville is well-known for its paranormal activity. Simply driving into the woods turns humans’ moods dark and causes pets to go wild. Drivers report movements in the shadows and strange sounds. Locals believe that the road developed an evil aura after it was cursed by Native Americans who were forced out of the area. Further fueling the eerie reputation are rumors of cult rituals taking place in the woods.

Archer Avenue, Chicago, Illinois

Archer Avenue cuts through one of Chicago’s most haunted areas. Between Resurrection Cemetery and St James-Sag church, the road passes by forest, lakes, and numerous graveyards. Phantom monks are said to haunt the area by St. James at Sag Bridge Church, a Gray Baby has been spotted at the Sacred Heart Cemetery, and phantom horsemen apparently cross the road at 95th Street. A ghostly hitchhiker, known as Resurrection Mary, has been sighted on Archer Avenue since the 1930s. The story goes that Mary was on her way home from the Willowbrook Ballroom late one night and was killed in a hit-and-run. She was buried in the Resurrection Cemetery in the same dress she wore that fateful night. Ever since then, she has waited for a ride by the side of the road. Drivers who stop to give her a lift find that she disappears the moment they reach the cemetery.

Haynesville Woods, Maine

It’s a stretch of road up north in Maine
That’s never ever ever seen a smile
If they’d buried all them truckers lost in them woods
There’d be a tombstone every mile

Those lines come from the 1965 song “A Tombstone Every Mile” by country singer Dick Curless, who warns truck drivers to steer clear of Route 2A through Maine’s Haynesville Woods. In the winter months, the road is extremely treacherous and, unsurprisingly, it’s the setting for several ghost sightings. One tale features a woman who pleads for help following a car crash. Stop to assist her, and you’ll feel a morbid chill before she disappears. Another story says that the road is haunted by a small girl who was hit by a truck.

Shades of Death Road, New Jersey

If ever there were a road sign to make you pull a U-turn, it’s the one that reads “Shades of Death Road” in Warren County, New Jersey. Exactly how the road got its name is up for debate. Some believe it is because of the highwaymen who once plied their trade along it, or several lynchings that took place nearby. Others say it’s down to the nearby swamps that led to regular malaria outbreaks, causing death and heartache.

Three vicious murders took place during the 1920s and 1930s along the road, which only increases the scare factor, as do a number of fatal car accidents. If that weren’t scary enough, local wildcats have been known to attack travelers, while mysterious mists and unusual orbs of light are further signs of paranormal activity.

Clinton Road, New Jersey

The hauntings on this New Jersey road have even made it to the big screen as the subject of the 2019 movie Clinton Road, in which a firefighter’s wife goes missing. In the film, he hires a witch doctor to contact her spirit, but in the real world it’s much easier to make contact with “the other side.” On Ghost Boy Bridge, it’s said that if you leave a quarter in the middle of the road, it will be returned by the ghost of a boy who drowned in the water below. Ghost rangers, a ghoulish Camaro, and strange creatures from the nearby abandoned Jungle Habitat zoo have also been seen. In 1983, the victim of a gangland murder was found in the woods close to the road, further enshrining Clinton Road in folklore. 

Route 666: Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona

Of course, if you number a road 666, people are going to associate it with Beelzebub himself. The so-called Devil’s Highway used to run from Utah into Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah and was known as one of America’s most dangerous roads. Although there are claims of phantom semi trucks, the real reason the road turned out to be so hazardous was that it’s so straight that drivers would lose concentration, while a lack of policing also led to higher speeds. Still, the ghost stories wouldn’t disappear, so in 2003 the road’s name was changed to Route 491.
